messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Marcus

Marcus was twenty-four when he first arrived in Syria with a humanitarian relief organization, driven by the conviction that he could help. For three months he moved between camps and makeshift clinics, documenting need, distributing supplies, and bearing witness to suffering he had not known existed. On his final week, a mortar struck a school where he had spent the morning helping distribute blankets to children. He was two blocks away when it happened—close enough to feel the concussion, close enough to hear the screaming that followed. He ran toward it with others, stepping over rubble, finding small bodies. One girl, perhaps seven, was still conscious when he reached her, her left leg severed below the knee. He held her hand as volunteers carried her away. He never learned her name or what became of her.

That was five years ago. Marcus returned home and tried to move forward. He became a jeweler, work that demanded precision and focus—something he thought might anchor him. For the first two years, the memories stayed mostly dormant, surfacing only at night or when he was alone. But gradually the boundary between then and now began to erode. A child crying in the grocery store—his daughter's voice, the one he'd held—would flood back with such force that his heart would race uncontrollably, and he would find himself unable to breathe, certain that if his pulse didn't slow he would die. The memory came not as a distant recollection but as an immediate, overwhelming presence, more vivid and real than any ordinary memory of his own apartment or his work. When his own heartbeat accelerated, the memory would follow instantly, as though his body had become a trigger for the full traumatic scene to replay without warning.

These episodes frightened him profoundly. Marcus had come to believe that the world was fundamentally unsafe, that danger was constant and often invisible. In any room, he found himself scanning for weapons—the letter opener on a client's desk, the heavy bookend, the way light caught on broken glass. He felt unsafe unless his back was against a wall where he could see the entire space, and even then, the safety felt fragile, conditional on his vigilance. When people told him he was safe, that he was home now, that the war was thousands of miles away, something in him rejected their reassurance entirely. He was certain that they simply didn't understand the reality he inhabited—that safety was an illusion people told themselves.

To manage the overwhelming memories and the fear, Marcus developed strategies that seemed to help in the moment. When the panic came, he would force himself to think only positive thoughts, reminding himself that it could have been worse, that he had survived, that others had suffered more. The reframing felt necessary—a way to contain the terror. But the relief never lasted long. Within hours, sometimes minutes, the effort of maintaining that positive stance would collapse, and the memory would return with renewed intensity, as though his mind had been holding its breath and could only exhale by flooding him with the full weight of what he'd witnessed. The harder he tried to suppress the image, the more insistently it would intrude. When he caught himself scanning the room again for threats, or when his heart began to race, the memory would be waiting there, ready to emerge. His constant vigilance—checking surroundings, noticing potential weapons, positioning himself defensively—seemed to reinforce the very belief that danger was everywhere, making the threats feel more real and more imminent.

At twenty-nine, Marcus works alone most days in his workshop, which suits him. He no longer goes to social gatherings. He has not been in a relationship since his return. Six months ago, a colleague touched his shoulder without warning to show him a design, and Marcus's entire body seized with such terror that he nearly struck the man. That moment—the realization that his own body could betray him, that an innocent gesture could trigger a response he couldn't control—finally pushed him to seek help. He sits now in the therapist's office with his back to the corner, and he tells her that what frightens him most is that the memory will never feel like the past, that he will spend the rest of his life unable to distinguish between what happened then and what is happening now.
